## How to use the RIBA Plan of Work during a project

The RIBA Plan of Work 2020 can be used at the start of a project as a practical roadmap. It will help structure the tasks required at each stage, from initial briefing through to completion and use.

As a project progresses, the Plan of Work is then used as a coordination and communication tool between the client, architect, consultants, and contractor. It can be referenced when preparing appointment documents, agreeing on services and [fees](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/architects-fees-in-the-uk/), and setting out information requirements at each stage.

By aligning the Core Tasks at each stage with meetings, deliverables, and approvals, the team can manage risks and track progress. They can use the plan to ensure all Core Tasks and Statutory Processes are complete before moving on to the next phase of the project.

The full detailed plan in the following image gives information on the Core Tasks at each stage:

![RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7 "RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart published by The RIBA")![RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/RIBA-plan-of-work-2020.jpg "RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart published by The RIBA")

![RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7 "RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart published by The RIBA")
![RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/RIBA-plan-of-work-2020.jpg "RIBA plan of work 2020, project stages chart published by The RIBA")

RIBA Plan of Work 2020 Credit: RIBA

On the vertical axes of the Plan of Work (to the left of the page), the following considerations are suggested for each of the eight stages:

In the following design stages section, we will discuss each stage of the plan in detail.

## RIBA Plan Of Work: stages in detail

### Stage 0

The first stage of the Plan of Work loosely outlines a project brief and identifies the defining criteria of your project, your priorities and your design ambition. This stage is often pre-appointment, so it provides an opportunity for the client to get a sense of what the architect has to offer. This includes assessing their experience and portfolio.

Initial site appraisals can then be undertaken, incorporating any feedback from potential previous projects. You may wish to engage a planning consultant to appraise any relevant planning policy considerations.

Stage 0 is particularly important for you to set the tone of the project and for us together to:

The client should assess their priorities in terms of [cost](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/how-much-cost-to-build-a-house/), size, quality and time. A [programme](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/what-is-a-construction-programme/) can be produced illustrating each step of the process, including briefing, design, construction and handover. Consider whether there are any important milestones or foreseeable breaks in the programme. It may be worth considering whether interior design, landscaping or other design consultants may be required, even at this early stage.

Is the project best suited for [refurbishment](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/home-retrofitting/), new-build or a combination? This decision will take into account sustainability, living comfort, budget limitations, local planning policy and site context.

### Stage 0 for a residential project

For a smaller-scale project such as a residential extension, this stage might simply involve considering whether an extension is actually needed. You might want to consider the following:

Your architect can then help you to map your project against each of the following seven stages (1–7), ensuring that key tasks, such as concept design, planning, technical design, construction, and handover, are considered.

Your architect will help you to adapt the rest of the RIBA Plan of Work to suit the project size, type, specific procurement route, programme, and your desired level of client involvement. You can use the stage descriptions to check that nothing essential is missed.

[![An architect-designed house in Dorset, an example of The RIBA Plan of Work applied to a coastal home](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)![An architect-designed house in Dorset, an example of The RIBA Plan of Work applied to a coastal home](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/new-house-dorset-architects.jpg)](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/dorset-beach-house/)

![An architect-designed house in Dorset, an example of The RIBA Plan of Work applied to a coastal home](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)
![An architect-designed house in Dorset, an example of The RIBA Plan of Work applied to a coastal home](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/new-house-dorset-architects.jpg)

[Dorset Beach House](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/dorset-beach-house/) by Architecture for London

### RIBA Stage 1

Preparation and Briefing, as the name suggests, uses the information gathered at the previous stage to draft an initial project brief:

Usually, this will also include any relevant feasibility studies, site/building surveys and an initial risk assessment. An appraisal of the project cost is also outlined, along with forming a procurement strategy. Both of these will be informed by experience from previous similar projects.

Every stage of the RIBA Plan of Work incorporates sustainability checkpoints. It is also particularly important to include a [sustainability strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_architecture) from the start of a project.

Pre-app planning discussions with the local authority may be useful at the end of stage one. This early engagement can help to guide the design. Early discussions may also increase the likelihood of the council supporting any proposal in a planning application at stage 3.

Key tasks in Stage 1 include the assembly of the project team and defining the structure, roles and responsibilities.

### RIBA Stage 2

Stages 2, 3 and 4 are the main design stages of the RIBA plan of work. Stage 2 is Concept Design, and this is likely the stage at which the client receives the first visualisations or drawings of the design ideas developed from the project brief. There may be meetings, workshops or general correspondence to discuss iterations of the concept design.

The Final Project Brief is defined from a review of the initial brief. This administrative exercise includes defining how the Project Strategies will affect the design process:

The concept design also often includes an initial proposal for structural design, building services and specifications. These can be used for the Cost Information (defining all the costs associated with the project).

When the design reaches RIBA stages 2/3, a programme review may be useful. Depending on the nature of the design, third-party consultants may be approached.

This is also a stage at which it could be of interest to consider relevant Research & Development. For example, there may be advancements made in project-related fields, interesting materials or new solutions that may improve the design.

[![Interior retail architect design in Westminster, London with curtains and stainless steel](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)![Interior retail architect design in Westminster, London with curtains and stainless steel](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Interior-retail-architect-design.jpg)](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/fisher-paykel-showroom/)

![Interior retail architect design in Westminster, London with curtains and stainless steel](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)
![Interior retail architect design in Westminster, London with curtains and stainless steel](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Interior-retail-architect-design.jpg)

[Fisher & Paykel Showroom](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/fisher-paykel-showroom/) by Architecture for London

### RIBA Stage 3

The Spatial Coordination stage is where a coordinated design takes form. Continuing from a settled concept design, the project is drawn up more clearly in CAD and developed alongside structural design, building services and a cost exercise. Cost information is usually finalised at the end of RIBA stage 3.

As a result of this coordination, the design may change in detail throughout stage 3, but always referring back to the Project Brief and Project Objectives.

Due to the adaptability of the RIBA Plan of Work, submission time for planning consent may vary between the stages, but it usually occurs during or at the end of design stage 3.

A [planning application](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/the-cost-of-a-planning-application/) requires a degree of detail in drawings and information that is dependent on the type of project. In general, it will include:

If your building is listed or in a conservation area, a [Design and Access Statement](https://www.planningportal.co.uk/faqs/faq/51/what_is_a_design_and_access_statement) will be required. This document explains the need for the development and how it takes its surroundings into account. The D&A statement is usually prepared by the Architect. If the building is listed, an application for [listed building consent](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/listed-building-architect/) (with an additional Heritage Statement) will also be required.

### RIBA Stage 4

Technical Design is a refinement of the existing design, essentially preparing the necessary drawings and documentation for tendering. It often involves approaching relevant specialist [subcontractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcontractor), such as a glazing manufacturer or joinery firm.

The level of detail required may vary according to the type of procurement and the nature of the project: will the drawings be used for actual construction on site? Is this being provided directly by the subcontractors?

As with planning, the stage at which the tender process occurs may vary; traditionally, it is done at the end of stage 4, however. This is mainly due to the level of detail needed by contractors to price their work correctly.

The Architect’s services, to submit for tendering, include:

The Contractor is generally selected and employed by the client. One of the benefits of working with an experienced architect, such as Architecture for London, is that we can suggest suitable contractors, sub-contractors, and consultants.

[![london house extension brick with bespoke bench seat and kitchen island in stone and a polished concrete floor](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)![london house extension brick with bespoke bench seat and kitchen island in stone and a polished concrete floor](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/london-house-extension-brick.jpg)](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/de-beauvoir-house-extension/)

![london house extension brick with bespoke bench seat and kitchen island in stone and a polished concrete floor](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)
![london house extension brick with bespoke bench seat and kitchen island in stone and a polished concrete floor](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/london-house-extension-brick.jpg)

[De Beauvoir House](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/de-beauvoir-house-extension/) by Architecture for London

### RIBA Stage 5

RIBA stage 5 signifies the start of Construction. The design is generally considered complete at the start of the Construction stage. The Architect is on hand to deal with any Design Queries. Our role at this stage will vary. In some cases, particularly where a compressed programme is key, stages 4 and 5 will overlap or progress simultaneously.

The simultaneous progression of stages 4 and 5 means that work on site can begin faster, although there may be more pricing uncertainty for the contractor due to unresolved design details. It should be noted that pricing uncertainty can lead to more [provisional sums](http://constructionblog.practicallaw.com/ask-the-team-what-are-provisional-sums/) appearing in the contractor’s tender return. There is, therefore, often a trade-off for the client between speed and price certainty.

Construction effectively means that the Contractor will take possession of the site and carry out the works as listed in the Schedule of Work and the building contract. This includes both manufacturing off-site and construction on-site.

### Stage 5 Contract Administration

Architecture for London can advise on the nature of the contract or act as Contract Administrator. Contract Administrator duties include:

An Architect’s Instruction (Or a Contract Administrator’s Instruction) can, among other things, be issued when it is required to:

![arches house extension islington](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)
![arches house extension islington](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/arches-house-extension-islington.jpg)

### RIBA Stage 6

Stage 6 of the RIBA Plan of Works is the Handover phase. This stage concludes all aspects of the Building Contract, including rectifying any defects on the Contractor’s part and producing the final certificate on the Contract Administrator’s part. In some situations, it may include commissioning to ensure the building functions properly.

Architects, when acting as contract administrator, may help the Contractor with a schedule of defects, but ultimately it is the Contractor’s responsibility to ensure that the works comply with the drawings, specification and contract documents. A retention sum may be held from the Contractor, repayable after the Defects Liability Period.

### Rectification Period

After the building has been handed over, the Defects Liability Period (or Rectification Period) begins, normally lasting between 6 months and a year. The contractor must report and remedy any defects found within this time.

If defects are found after the Rectification Period, they are termed latent defects. At this point, the client no longer has the right to insist that the contractor make good any defects. If the contractor is unwilling to return and make good, the client will need to take legal action to win compensation for damages.

The ability to take action for negligence or non-compliance with the contract lasts for 6 years from the completion date of most building contracts.

The building owner’s manual is handed over. For a smaller, residential project, this might be a simple homeowner pack with instructions on use and maintenance. A homeowner client may need a demonstration of the sustainability principles, including airtightness, ventilation and how to use any controls on the MVHR unit.

### RIBA Stage 7

The in-use stage of the RIBA Plan of Work exists as a form of aftercare service for the Client. This may include any requests for as-built drawings, any discussions regarding [future alterations](https://architectureforlondon.com/project/work-in-progress/) or additional work, or general advice on:

These services, if required, should be outlined in the initial appointment agreement.

Architecture for London is always interested in hearing how the building performs. There may be a feedback workshop, and we are happy to take comments from the client on board, as these are valuable for future projects as well.

Monitoring the building’s energy performance is key at RIBA stage 7, to check whether the sustainability strategy has been successful and the building is performing as expected.

To ensure optimal performance, adjustments to the building’s services may be required. Advising the client on how to best use the building in accordance with the sustainability strategy is also crucial. A highly insulated building with an airtight layer and MVHR is of little use if windows are always left open.

![RIBA Plan of Work: architect designed rear extension in London](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)
![RIBA Plan of Work: architect designed rear extension in London](https://architectureforlondon.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/architect-london-rear-extension-2.jpg)

## The RIBA Plan of Work 2020 changes at a glance

The RIBA Plan of Work 2020 retains the familiar eight stages (0–7) from the 2013 version but refines the language, tasks and information exchanges at each step. It responds to current practice by better accommodating design‑and‑build procurement, off‑site manufacturing and digital coordination between the client, architect and wider team.

Compared with 2013, the 2020 update places greater weight on sustainability outcomes from Stage 0 through to in‑use evaluation at Stage 7. It also introduces new terminology (for example, renaming ‘Developed Design’ as ‘Spatial Coordination’) and supports a range of optional overlays, such as Sustainability, Conservation and Passivhaus, so the framework can be tailored to specific project types and priorities.

## Recent updates: optional overlays

There have been several post-2020 updates or ‘overlays’ as the RIBA calls them. These documents provide additional, specialist guidance that sits alongside the core Plan of Work. Some key examples of these are as follows:

### Passivhaus Overlay (February 2023)

This overlay aligns the RIBA Plan of Work with [Passivhaus](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/passivhaus-architects-london/) principles, offering step-by-step guidance on how to integrate energy efficiency, airtightness, and thermal comfort targets throughout all project stages. It helps design teams embed performance-led thinking from the earliest briefing stages through to post-occupancy.

### Engagement Overlay (January 2024)

Focused on consultation and communication, this overlay sets out best practice for engaging with clients, users, and wider stakeholders. It emphasises inclusive design processes, clear decision-making, and transparent dialogue across the project timeline, from initial briefing to building handover and use.

### Smart Building Overlay (February 2024)

This overlay provides guidance on integrating digital technologies, data strategies, and building automation into projects. It supports architects in coordinating smart systems with the wider design, ensuring that digital infrastructure, user experience, and long-term management are considered from the outset.

Together, these overlays illustrate how the RIBA Plan of Work continues to evolve beyond 2020, offering targeted guidance that addresses performance, engagement, and technology in contemporary architectural practice.

## RIBA Stages for London residential projects

When working with smaller residential projects, the Pan of Work is often simplified out of cost necessity. Residential projects tend to have lower budgets, and therefore, an architect’s role is often condensed to reduce fee expenditure.

With our smaller residential projects (for example, a house extension with a budget of £200,000 or less), we might not take a formal contract administration role at stage 5 at all. Our work at stage 5 might be on a simple time charge basis, visiting the site as required and assisting the client and contractor informally as required.

Architecture for London usually arranges the work stages into three main segments for simplification. These three segments are useful when calculating our [fee proposals](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/architects-fees-in-the-uk/), as the project can be split into three simplified parts, each of which may be undertaken independently:

At Architecture for London, we offer our clients services at all RIBA work stages.

### Keeping costs under control for residential projects

For every project, we issue a clear scope, fee breakdown and project programme so you understand what is included at each stage before we begin. At each RIBA stage, we:

• Review the construction budget and assess any cost risks.

• Coordinate with cost consultants (we have an in-house cost consultant) so that design decisions are informed by up-to-date pricing.

• Update the programme to reflect any new planning, procurement or site information.

## RIBA Plan of Work: a conclusion

The RIBA Plan of Work is intended as a guiding document; ultimately, its strength lies in its adaptability and the architect’s ability to make it work for you – and your project. A Plan of Work toolbox Excel file can be downloaded and customised for your building project [here](https://www.architecture.com/-/media/GatherContent/Test-resources-page/Additional-Documents/2020RIBAPlanofWorktoolboxFeb2020xlsx.xlsx). This document can feed into your project’s [construction phase plan](https://architectureforlondon.com/news/what-is-a-construction-phase-plan/).

The 2020 version of the Plan of Work reflects the RIBA’s commitment for projects to be net-zero carbon by 2030 with a new sustainability project strategy. At stage zero, the plan encourages the development of “high-level, measurable, ambitious and unambiguous project Sustainability Outcomes”.

The RIBA Plan of Work and additional useful information about the RIBA stages can be found [here](https://www.riba.org/work/insights-and-resources/riba-plan-of-work/).

If you are planning a house extension or refurbishment and need help navigating the RIBA stages, contact Architecture for London for a free 30‑minute consultation: 020 3637 4236

## FAQ about the RIBA Plan of Work & Project Stages

### Why use the RIBA Plan of Work?

The Plan’s strength lies in its clear presentation of the tasks involved in each stage of a construction project. It is also adaptable: a customised Plan of Work can be downloaded for a particular building project.

### What stage is planning permission?

A planning application is usually made during, or at the end of Stage 3 (Spatial Coordination). Stage 4 (Technical Design) often begins, at risk, before the planning consent is actually received.

### What stage is Building Regulations?

The Building Regulations are considered at nearly all RIBA stages. However, much of the work happens during Stage 4. This includes the submission of Building Regulations drawings and information to either Building Control or an Approved Inspector. Site monitoring for building regulations compliance continues at Stage 5.

### Can I use the RIBA Plan of Work for design and build?

Yes, the Plan of Work can be used for design and build projects. It is a flexible framework that can be adapted to different procurement routes.

### What is the difference between Stage 4 and Stage 5?

Stage 4 (Technical Design) is where the architect and design team finalise detailed drawings, specifications and information for pricing. Stage 5 (Manufacturing and Construction) is when the contractor takes over the site and carries out the building works in accordance with the designs and the building contract.

## The RIBA Plan of Work

*This is part of a series of articles looking at [The Digital Plan of Work](/our-tools/digital-plan-of-work)*

[The RIBA Plan of Work](https://www.architecture.com/knowledge-and-resources/resources-landing-page/riba-plan-of-work) was initiated in 1963 as a framework for architects to use on projects. Over the years, it has become an industry-wide tool. It explains the expected outcomes, core tasks and information exchanges throughout the life of a construction project.

The 2020 version of the Plan of Work includes an ‘Information Exchanges’ taskbar, as shown below in Figure 1. The information produced at the end of a stage then influences the decisions and the work required throughout the next stage. For example, the ‘Business Case’ at the end of Stage 0 then informs the ‘Project Budget’ that is developed as part of Stage 1. With respect to the more structured information requirements, the ‘Responsibility Matrix’ and the ‘Information Requirements’ delivered at the end of Stage 1 are critical to the success of the project.

![](/Content/images/my-nbs-placeholder.png)

Figure 1.1 - The ‘Information Exchanges’ taskbar within the RIBA Plan of Work.

(Click the image to see in more detail)

## The RIBA Plan of Work Overview

Although this article focuses on the planning and delivery of information requirements, the wider aspects of the RIBA Plan of Work are covered in the free ‘Overview’ guide. The guide looks at three main areas:

[Download The RIBA Plan of Work Overview](https://www.architecture.com/knowledge-and-resources/resources-landing-page/riba-plan-of-work)

## The RIBA Plan of Work Toolbox

As part of the launch of the RIBA Plan of Work 2013, NBS and the RIBA worked together with respect to the digital aspects of the Plan of Work. NBS also worked with RIBA and other industry bodies to develop an online digital plan of work tool as part of the Innovate UK-funded BIM Toolkit. NBS and RIBA worked closely together to align both.

The online version within the BIM Toolkit was retired in June 2022. NBS recommends using the RIBA Plan of Work Toolbox for defining **who** is in the project team and **what** each party in the project team needs to do. The Toolbox contains template content for a ‘Project Roles Table’, a ‘Responsibility Matrix‘and ‘Multidisciplinary Schedules of Services’.
The Responsibility Matrix allows for the planning of aspects of design, giving clear responsibility for delivery at each stage, and indicators for level of detail (LOD) and level of information (LOI).

Clarity is also needed on where the design responsibilities lie between the design team and any specialist subcontractors. This is not the same as simply setting the procurement route. Traditional projects may have elements of specialist subcontractor design where descriptive information is needed. Equally, design-and-build projects may have elements of prescriptive information where the client would like the design team to have responsibility for certain system and product decisions. With this in mind, it is essential that a Responsibility Matrix is set up prior to the design stages of a project. Clearly, the Responsibility Matrix will be updated as the project progresses, and it is essential that this is reviewed at the start of the technical design stage of a project (RIBA Stage 4) so it is clear who is producing the final information for construction.

The screenshots below illustrate how a Responsibility Matrix in the RIBA Plan of Work Toolbox may develop throughout the project timeline. Click to view a larger version of each screenshot.

### Responsibility Matrix – prior to the design stages

Figure 2.1 shows an example Responsibility Matrix within the RIBA Plan of Work Toolbox developed prior to the design stages. This considers the design practice ABC Architects planning the design prior to the procurement strategy being known. Note that:

![](/Content/images/my-nbs-placeholder.png)

Figure 2.1 – Example Responsibility Matrix within the RIBA Plan of Work Toolbox, developed prior to design stages

(Click the image to see in more detail)

### Responsibility Matrix – prior to the technical design stage

Figure 2.2 shows the same example Responsibility Matrix prior to the technical design stage of the project. This example demonstrates a design-and-build project, where the main contractor has not novated ABC Architects, and the designers (DEF Architecture) are now part of the design team. The specialist subcontractor XYZ Roofing is now also named. Note that:

![](/Content/images/my-nbs-placeholder.png)

Figure 2.2 – Updated Responsibility Matrix prior to technical design stage

(Click the image to see in more detail)

### Specification planning – prior to the technical design stage

Figure 2.3 shows the same example specification summary sheet within NBS Chorus prior to the technical design stage of the project. This shows how expert platforms such as Chorus can add further detail over and above the Responsibility Matrix developed in tools such as Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets. Note that:

![](/Content/images/my-nbs-placeholder.png)

Figure 2.3 – Specification summary sheet in NBS Chorus reflecting information requirements detailed in the Responsibility Matrix

(Click the image to see in more detail)

At the end of the technical design stage, final requirements for handover information will be known. The specification itself will list these system completion tasks and information requirements. A master information delivery plan should then be developed to reflect these requirements, and in this further LOD and LOI bandings for the construction and handover stages of the project may be referenced.

The RIBA Plan of Work is intended as a multidisciplinary tool that is used by the lead designer. Further discipline-specific guidance is provided by other institutions. These are linked to below:

The RIBA Plan of Work sets out the need for clear information exchanges and the responsibilities for delivery, but does not provide guidance in terms of more detailed information management. The resources at the UK BIM Framework website sets out the approach for implementing BIM in the UK using the framework for managing information provided by the ISO 19650 series. It includes: the published standards called upon to implement BIM in the UK; the UK BIM Guidance Framework; and useful links to other resources.
